newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says budget offers education legacy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says budget offers education legacy.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday urged Congress to pass the balanced budget agreement, calling it an historic accord that offers the greatest increase in funding for education in 30 years.

Clinton used his weekly radio address to the nation to pay tribute to Republicans as well as Democrats for their efforts to hammer out the final details of the budget accord, which he said "expands opportunity through education."
The agreement goes to both houses of Congress for approval next week. "Pass the balanced budget and pass the biggest and best education bill in America's history," Clinton said.

"To me, the heart of this balanced budget agreement is its historic commitment to education," he said. "Education has always been at the heart of opportunity in America. It's the embodiment of everything we have to do to prepare for the 21st Century."

"This agreement includes the most significant increase in education funding in 30 years," he said. "Even more important, it provides the largest single increase in higher education since the G.I. Bill in 1945, more than 50 years ago."

Clinton praised the accord -- finalised on Thursday after intense haggling between the White House and congressional leaders -- for expanding opportunity "so that we can keep the American Dream alive for all our children."
The agreement, which seeks to balance the federal budget by 2002, includes a commitment sought by Clinton for $35 billion in education tax credits and deductions.
Funding was included for many of Clinton's pet projects, including the "America Reads" programme to mobilise volunteer tutors to ensure that every 8-year-old can read.

It also provides money for the Technology Literacy Initiative, intended to connect every classroom and school library to the Internet by 2000; and for the HOPE Scholarship for tuition tax credit, designed to make the first two years of college as universal as high school.

Franklin Raines, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, told CNN's "Inside Politics" that details were still being worked out on a broad-based cut in the capital gains tax, a high priority for Republicans.
"We've got to figure out, though, how we take all of these demands and squeeze them into a very tight budget for tax cuts," Raines said.
He declined to estimate by how much the capital gains tax, now at 28 percent, would be reduced, but said the White House would keep "an open mind as to exactly how it's structured."
Raines predicted that a majority of Democrats would support the balanced budget deal, and said the agreement would likely win support from the Congressional Black Caucus as well.

The agreement provides for total spending reductions of $304 billion over five years, including slowing the growth of projected Medicare spending by $115 billion and Medicaid by $14 billion. It also includes net tax cuts of $85 billion through 2002.
In the Republican radio response, Representative Rick Lazio of New York promoted House passage on Wednesday of a bill to overhaul the public housing programme.
The bill would scrap the landmark Housing Act of 1937 and end many federal regulations. Local housing authorities would be given more authority to run the nation's 13,200 public housing developments.
"This is about restoring mixed-income neighbourhoods where working families serve as role models," said Lazio, who has spearheaded the drive for the legislation.
The Clinton administration and many Democrats oppose the bill, saying it would throw the very poor out of public housing in favour of moderate-income residents.
